resources.string: In this lesson, you are the Earth
You will turn around on the spot, no walking. Keep 1 metre around you clear, or sit on a swivel chair. If you step outside the safe area, the headset shows the room again.

string-array.name: intro_titles
string-array.item: This is the Sun
Your head is the Earth
This is the Moon, it goes round with you

string-array.name: intro_bodies
string-array.item: A lamp 4 metres away, at eye height. It is the only light in this room: everything you will see is lit by it.
The ring on the floor has eight marks. Each phase you find lights one of them.
At arm\'s length, a little above the Sun. Turn left on the spot and watch how much of its lit half you can see.

string-array.name: phase_names
string-array.item: New Moon
Waxing Crescent
First Quarter
Waxing Gibbous
Full Moon
Waning Gibbous
Third Quarter
Waning Crescent

string-array.name: phase_dos
string-array.item: Face the Sun
Turn a little to the left
Keep turning until the Sun is on your right
A bit more to the left
Turn your back to the Sun
Keep turning left
Turn until the Sun is on your left
Almost back to the Sun

string-array.name: phase_whys
string-array.item: Its dark side faces you and the Sun is in your eyes, so you can barely see it.
A thin bright edge appears on the right. It\'s the sliver you see in the west after sunset.
The right half is lit. It looks like a half, but the Moon is only a quarter of the way round.
More than half is lit, and it\'s still growing.
The whole lit face points at you. The Moon passes a little below your head, missing Earth\'s shadow.
The lit part starts shrinking; this time the right side goes dark first.
The left half is lit: the mirror of First Quarter.
Only a thin sliver on the left, seen in the east before dawn. Turn back to the Sun and it is New Moon again.

resources.string: ↷ Too far, come back a little
The Sun moved to your right. Turn back a little.
One full turn = one cycle of phases, about 29.5 days. Half the Moon is always lit; what changes is how much of that half you see.
Why isn\'t there an eclipse every month?
The Moon\'s path is tilted (shown as 10° here; really about 5°), so at New Moon it passes above the Sun. Flatten the orbit and see.

string-array.name: eclipse_names
string-array.item: Solar Eclipse
Lunar Eclipse

string-array.name: eclipse_dos
string-array.item: With the orbit flat, face the Sun
With the orbit flat, turn your back to the Sun

string-array.name: eclipse_whys
string-array.item: The Moon blocks the Sun and only the corona glows, because they look about the same size in the sky.
The Moon slips into Earth\'s shadow, your head. Earth\'s air bends a little red light into the shadow, so it glows dim copper.

resources.string: The Sun on your right, the right half lit: that is First Quarter.
The Moon keeps going left, the lit part grows, and a quarter of the way round it is First Quarter.
Back to the Sun, the whole lit face towards you: Full Moon.
At Third Quarter the left half is lit, so the light comes from the left.
You had to flatten the orbit before the Moon could cover the Sun.
Third Quarter is lit on the left; First Quarter on the right.
Based on the NASA/JPL Education classroom activity "Moon Phases". The lit side is drawn as seen from the northern hemisphere. The Moon\'s surface is drawn by the app, not a photo.
